newsitem.title: UK: Funding boost for UK Labour as union allies fume.
newsitem.headline: Funding boost for UK Labour as union allies fume.

text.p: At the end of a week of fierce rows with its trade union allies, Britain's Labour party received a welcome boost on Saturday when a businessmen pledged 500,000 pounds ($777,600) to the party.

Bob Gavron, former chairman of printing company St Ives Plc, said Labour leader Tony Blair was transforming the party's relations with business and was more committed than the ruling Conservatives to helping budding entrepreneurs.

"I believe that Britain is in need of change and I like the fresh and enthusiastic approach of Tony Blair and his team, which is in strong contrast to the obvious weariness of the present government," Gavron said.

Insurance tycoon Matthew Harding earlier this month donated one million pounds ($1.56 million) to Labour, which receives most of its funds from trade unions and has traditionally been perceived as hostile to business.
"The days when the Tories (Conservatives) were automatically the party of business are over," Gavron said.
As business warms to Blair, his ties with the trade unions that created Labour nearly a century ago are rapidly cooling.

This week's annual conference of the Trades Union Congress (TUC), the movement's umbrella body, was dominated by reports that Labour was considering how to crack down on public sector strikes and might even one day sever all links with the unions.
Although Blair and his aides reassured union leaders that the talk was unfounded, TUC General Secretary John Monks said delegates were shaken by the speculation.
"Sometimes Labour seem keener to stress what they won't do rather than what they will," Monks writes in Sunday's News of the World newspaper.

Despite the storm, Blair's lieutenants are confident that headlines portraying Labour as tough on unions will help woo the floating centre-ground voters it needs to win the forthcoming general election, now at most eight months away.
Labour, in opposition since 1979, enjoy an opinion poll lead of more than 20 percentage points over Prime Minister John Major's Conservatives.
